A_target.statement:
Let $P$ be the [[Definition:Transition Matrix|transition matrix]] of an [[Definition:Irreducible Markov Chain|irreducible]] [[Definition:Aperiodic Markov Chain|aperiodic]] [[Definition:Markov Chain|Markov chain]] on a finite state space.
Then there is a [[Definition:Unique|unique]] [[Definition:Stationary Distribution|stationary distribution]] $\pi$ with $\pi P = \pi$, and $\mu P^n \to \pi$ for every distribution $\mu$.

B_source.statement:
Let $K \subseteq \R^n$ be [[Definition:Compact Space|compact]] and [[Definition:Convex Set (Vector Space)|convex]], and $f: K \to K$ [[Definition:Continuous Mapping|continuous]].
Then there exists $x \in K$ with $\map f x = x$.

substitutions.the compact convex set K: the simplex of probability distributions on the state space
substitutions.the continuous self-map f: right multiplication by the transition matrix P

derived.the fixed-point equation: the balance equation pi P = pi

validity_conditions: P must be stochastic so the simplex is mapped into itself
existence follows from compactness and convexity alone, but uniqueness requires irreducibility
convergence of mu P^n requires aperiodicity as well, and does not follow from the fixed point property
proof_plan:
The [[Definition:Simplex|simplex]] $\Delta$ of distributions is compact and convex.
As $P$ is [[Definition:Stochastic Matrix|stochastic]], $\mu \mapsto \mu P$ is a continuous map $\Delta \to \Delta$.
By the [[Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem]], there exists $\pi \in \Delta$ with $\pi P = \pi$.

By irreducibility and aperiodicity, $P^m$ has all entries strictly positive for some $m$.
By the [[Perron-Frobenius Theorem]], the eigenvalue $1$ of $P^m$ is simple, so $\pi$ is unique.

The remaining eigenvalues of $P$ have modulus $< 1$.
Hence:
:$\mu P^n \to \pi$
for every $\mu \in \Delta$.

By the [[Ergodic Theorem for Markov Chains|ergodic theorem]], $\pi_i$ is the long-run proportion of time spent in state $i$.
{{qed}}
